claim: Establishment of the pluripotent inner cell mass (ICM) in E3.5 blastocysts is linked with global DNA hypomethylation.
source: Accordingly, establishment of the pluripotent inner cell mass (ICM) in E3.5 blastocysts is linked with global DNA hypomethylation (Figure 1A) (Hackett et al., 2013a; Smith et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Hackett et al., 2013a; Smith et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2014) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Development of the ICM leads to the formation of primed postimplantation epiblast cells by E5.5–6.25.
source: Subsequent development of the ICM leads to the formation of primed postimplantation epiblast cells by E5.5–6.25, which are poised to initiate lineage-specification.
evidence: Based on established developmental biology knowledge and the manuscript's own observations.

claim: The developmental transition from ICM to epiblast is accompanied by genome-wide de novo DNA methylation.
source: This developmental transition is accompanied by epigenetic programming, including genome-wide de novo DNA methylation, and potentially accumulation of histone H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) and redistribution of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) (Figure 1A) (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The developmental transition from ICM to epiblast is accompanied by accumulation of histone H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2).
source: This developmental transition is accompanied by epigenetic programming, including genome-wide de novo DNA methylation, and potentially accumulation of histone H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) and redistribution of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) (Figure 1A) (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The developmental transition from ICM to epiblast is accompanied by redistribution of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3).
source: This developmental transition is accompanied by epigenetic programming, including genome-wide de novo DNA methylation, and potentially accumulation of histone H3 lysine 9 dimethylation (H3K9me2) and redistribution of histone H3 lysine 27 trimethylation (H3K27me3) (Figure 1A) (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Borgel et al., 2010; Leitch et al., 2013; Marks et al., 2012) and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: G9a (encoded by Ehmt2) is responsible for the establishment of H3K9me2.
source: Methyltransferase enzymes, G9a (encoded by Ehmt2) and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), respectively, are responsible for the establishment of these chromatin modifications (O'Carroll et al., 2001; Tachibana et al., 2002; 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (O'Carroll et al., 2001; Tachibana et al., 2002; 2005).

claim: Enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2) is responsible for the establishment of H3K27me3.
source: Methyltransferase enzymes, G9a (encoded by Ehmt2) and enhancer of zeste homolog 2 (EZH2), respectively, are responsible for the establishment of these chromatin modifications (O'Carroll et al., 2001; Tachibana et al., 2002; 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (O'Carroll et al., 2001; Tachibana et al., 2002; 2005).

claim: There is significant enrichment of H3K9me2 in the epiblast of E5.5 postimplantation embryos compared to E3.5 embryos.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) analysis of E3.5 and E5.5 embryos revealed significant enrichment of H3K9me2 in the epiblast of postimplantation embryos (Figure 1B,E).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1B,E.

claim: Accumulation of H3K9me2 coincides with increased levels of G9a and GLP enzymes.
source: Accumulation of this modification, which is dependent on G9a and its binding partner G9a-like protein (GLP), coincides with increased levels of the enzymes (Figure 1C,D,F,G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1C,D,F,G.

claim: Loss of G9a by E6.5 results in reduced levels of H3K9me2 modification.
source: Loss of G9a by E6.5 resulted in reduced levels of H3K9me2 modification, and an increase in apoptotic and non-proliferative cells as judged by IF staining for cleaved Caspase 3 and Ki67, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D.

claim: Loss of G9a by E6.5 results in an increase in apoptotic cells.
source: Loss of G9a by E6.5 resulted in reduced levels of H3K9me2 modification, and an increase in apoptotic and non-proliferative cells as judged by IF staining for cleaved Caspase 3 and Ki67, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing cleaved Caspase 3 staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D.

claim: Loss of G9a by E6.5 results in an increase in non-proliferative cells.
source: Loss of G9a by E6.5 resulted in reduced levels of H3K9me2 modification, and an increase in apoptotic and non-proliferative cells as judged by IF staining for cleaved Caspase 3 and Ki67, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing Ki67 staining in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,C,D.

claim: Loss of G9a leads to a developmental delay of mutant embryos by E7.5.
source: These changes led to a developmental delay of mutant embryos by E7.5 (Figure 2A,B), consistent with previous reports (Tachibana et al., 2002; Yamamizu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B and citations to previous reports (Tachibana et al., 2002; Yamamizu et al., 2012).

claim: RNA sequencing on Ehmt2−/− epiblasts at E6.25 revealed misregulation of 180 genes, of which 147 (~82%) are upregulated.
source: To gain further insight into the underlying causes of the phenotype, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) on individual Ehmt2−/− epiblasts at E6.25. This revealed misregulation of 180 genes, of which 147 (~82%) are upregulated (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1) (Log2[fold change[FC]]>1.4, p-value<0.05).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: Among the upregulated genes in Ehmt2−/− epiblasts, ~27% are located on the X chromosome.
source: Among the upregulated genes, ~27% of them were located on the X chromosome (p-value=1.6 × 10-15), notably in clusters of Xlr, Rhox and Mage-a genes.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis with statistical significance (p-value=1.6 × 10-15).

claim: Upregulated genes in Ehmt2−/− epiblasts show significant enrichment of gene ontology terms linked to hematopoiesis, sexual reproduction, and regulation of cell proliferation.
source: Consistent with the known functions of these clusters, we found significant enrichment of gene ontology (GO) terms linked to hematopoiesis, sexual reproduction, and regulation cell proliferation (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, and Figure 2—source data 2.

claim: A significant proportion of Ehmt2−/− cells show upregulation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor Cdkn1a.
source: A significant proportion of Ehmt2−/−cells showed upregulation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor Cdnkn1a, and late germline markers Asz1 and Rhox5 but not Pou5f1 (coding for OCT4) or Nanog (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: A significant proportion of Ehmt2−/− cells show upregulation of late germline markers Asz1 and Rhox5.
source: A significant proportion of Ehmt2−/−cells showed upregulation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor Cdnkn1a, and late germline markers Asz1 and Rhox5 but not Pou5f1 (coding for OCT4) or Nanog (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Ehmt2−/− cells do not show upregulation of Pou5f1 or Nanog.
source: A significant proportion of Ehmt2−/−cells showed upregulation of the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor Cdnkn1a, and late germline markers Asz1 and Rhox5 but not Pou5f1 (coding for OCT4) or Nanog (Figure 2E,F, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: The phenotypic effects of G9a loss cannot be attributed to a delayed exit from naïve pluripotency.
source: This indicates that, contrary to a previous report (Yamamizu et al., 2012), the phenotypic effects cannot be attributed to a delayed exit from naïve pluripotency.
evidence: Based on the observation that Pou5f1 and Nanog are not upregulated in Ehmt2−/− cells, contradicting a previous report (Yamamizu et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of G9a does not abrogate the establishment of a population of primordial germ cells (PGCs).
source: Furthermore, loss of G9a did not abrogate the establishment of a population of primordial germ cells (PGCs), as judged by the expression of AP2γ and OCT4, key germline regulators (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data showing AP2γ and OCT4 expression in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: G9a promotes growth of the embryo by repressing apoptotic and late germline genes.
source: These observations show that G9a promotes growth of the embryo by repressing apoptotic and late germline genes, but it does not affect the exit from naïve pluripotency and establishment of the PGC lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of G9a leads to upregulation of apoptotic and germline genes, increased apoptosis, and developmental delay.

claim: G9a does not affect the exit from naïve pluripotency.
source: These observations show that G9a promotes growth of the embryo by repressing apoptotic and late germline genes, but it does not affect the exit from naïve pluripotency and establishment of the PGC lineage.
evidence: Based on the observation that pluripotency markers Pou5f1 and Nanog are not affected in Ehmt2−/− cells.

claim: G9a does not affect the establishment of the PGC lineage.
source: These observations show that G9a promotes growth of the embryo by repressing apoptotic and late germline genes, but it does not affect the exit from naïve pluripotency and establishment of the PGC lineage.
evidence: Based on the observation that PGCs are established in Ehmt2−/− embryos as shown by AP2γ and OCT4 expression.

claim: RNA-seq on E6.25 Ezh2−/− epiblasts found upregulation of 165 transcripts and downregulation of 24 transcripts.
source: For this reason, we performed RNA-seq on individual E6.25 epiblasts lacking EZH2 (Ezh2−/−). We found upregulation of 165, and downregulation of 24 transcripts (Log2(FC)>1.4, p-value<0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B, Figure 2—source data 3)
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B and Figure 2—source data 3.

claim: Upregulated genes in Ezh2−/− epiblasts include homeobox and gastrulation-related genes, including Hoxd13 and Lefty2.
source: We found upregulation of 165, and downregulation of 24 transcripts (Log2(FC)>1.4, p-value<0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B, Figure 2—source data 3), among which were homeobox and gastrulation-related genes, including Hoxd13 and Lefty2, but pluripotency regulators such as Nanog and Pou5f1 were not affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B,C and Figure 2—source data 3,4.

claim: Pluripotency regulators Nanog and Pou5f1 are not affected in Ezh2−/− epiblasts.
source: We found upregulation of 165, and downregulation of 24 transcripts (Log2(FC)>1.4, p-value<0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B, Figure 2—source data 3), among which were homeobox and gastrulation-related genes, including Hoxd13 and Lefty2, but pluripotency regulators such as Nanog and Pou5f1 were not affected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C, Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C and Figure 2—source data 4.

claim: Only five significantly upregulated genes are shared between Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos.
source: Importantly, we only found five significantly upregulated genes that were shared between Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos.
evidence: Based on comparison of RNA-seq data from Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos.

claim: G9a and EZH2 stabilize silencing of distinct sets of germline, proliferation and developmental regulators.
source: Thus, G9a and EZH2 appear to stabilise silencing of distinct sets of germline, proliferation and developmental regulators, but neither of them has an effect on the pluripotency transcription programme in postimplantation embryos.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos show upregulation of different gene sets, with minimal overlap.

claim: Neither G9a nor EZH2 has an effect on the pluripotency transcription programme in postimplantation embryos.
source: Thus, G9a and EZH2 appear to stabilise silencing of distinct sets of germline, proliferation and developmental regulators, but neither of them has an effect on the pluripotency transcription programme in postimplantation embryos.
evidence: Based on the observation that pluripotency markers are not affected in either Ehmt2−/− or Ezh2−/− embryos.

claim: The enrichment of H3K9me2 in E6.25 epiblast is associated with low CpG content.
source: The enrichment of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications in E6.25 epiblast is associated with low and high CpG content, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The enrichment of H3K27me3 in E6.25 epiblast is associated with high CpG content.
source: The enrichment of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications in E6.25 epiblast is associated with low and high CpG content, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Naïve ESCs grown in 2i/LIF show spreading of H3K27me3 outside the CpG dense loci.
source: By contrast, naïve ESCs grown in 2i/LIF (2i/LIF ESCs) show spreading of H3K27me3 outside the CpG dense loci (Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Marks et al., 2012).

claim: There is redistribution of H3K27me3 in E6.25 epiblast relative to naïve ESCs.
source: Thus, there is redistribution of H3K27me3 in E6.25 epiblast, relative to both naïve ESCs and possibly ICM in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K27me3 is associated with high CpG content in E6.25 epiblast but spreads outside CpG dense loci in naïve ESCs.

claim: The association of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications on promoters is mutually exclusive.
source: The association of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications on promoters is mutually exclusive, since only 0.3% of them are enriched for both marks (Figure 3A, anticorrelation with Chi2 p-value=0.0024).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A with statistical significance (Chi2 p-value=0.0024).

claim: H3K9me2 is linked to high 5-methylcytosine (5meC) levels.
source: These differences are in line with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 being linked to high and low 5-methylcytosine (5meC) levels, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: H3K27me3 is linked to low 5-methylcytosine (5meC) levels.
source: These differences are in line with H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 being linked to high and low 5-methylcytosine (5meC) levels, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Both H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are linked to transcriptional repression.
source: Nonetheless, despite marking distinct chromatin regions, both H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are linked to transcriptional repression (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Gene repression is correlated with histone modification enrichment at promoters as well as in gene bodies.
source: Notably, this gene repression is correlated with histone modification enrichment at promoters as well as in gene bodies.
evidence: Based on analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: H3K9me2 modification in gene bodies could impede transcriptional elongation, splicing, or activity of regulatory elements.
source: The H3K9me2 modification in gene bodies could impede transcriptional elongation, splicing, or activity of regulatory elements (Allo et al., 2009).
evidence: Speculative statement supported by citation to published work (Allo et al., 2009).

claim: H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications in vivo are linked to distinct repressive chromatin states.
source: Our evidence suggests that H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 modifications in vivo are linked to distinct repressive chromatin states.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are mutually exclusive, associated with different CpG densities and DNA methylation levels.

claim: 1770 genes become activated in E6.25 epiblast compared to E3.5 ICM.
source: First, we identified genes that become robustly activated or repressed in E6.25 epiblasts relative to ICM (Figure 3D) (Log2(RPKM)<4, p-value<0.05, Log2(FC)>1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 1498 genes become repressed in E6.25 epiblast compared to E3.5 ICM.
source: First, we identified genes that become robustly activated or repressed in E6.25 epiblasts relative to ICM (Figure 3D) (Log2(RPKM)<4, p-value<0.05, Log2(FC)>1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Genes that become silenced by E6.25 are enriched for GO terms such as 'blastocyst formation' and 'STAT signalling regulation'.
source: For example, the transcripts that become silenced by the postimplantation stage (E6.25) are enriched for GO terms such as 'blastocyst formation' and 'STAT (Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription) signalling regulation' (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Genes repressed in E6.25 epiblast are generally enriched for H3K9me2 or H3K27me3, especially when they have high or intermediate CpG density, respectively.
source: These repressed genes are generally enriched for H3K9me2 or H3K27me3, especially when they have high or intermediate CpG density, respectively (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is transient expression of 5meC-sensitive germline genes at E3.5 that are subsequently repressed by E6.25.
source: Moreover, consistent with global DNA hypomethylation of the ICM, there is transient expression of 5meC-sensitive germline genes at E3.5 that are subsequently repressed by E6.25.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of global DNA hypomethylation at E3.5 and subsequent repression of germline genes by E6.25.

claim: Genes activated in E6.25 epiblast include 'neural tube' and 'polarized epithelium' genes.
source: On the other hand, genes activated in E6.25 epiblast include 'neural tube' and 'polarized epithelium' genes (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Both activated and repressed genes in E6.25 epiblast are enriched for regulators of transcription, embryonic development and metabolic processes.
source: Finally, both activated and repressed genes are enriched for regulators of transcription, embryonic development and metabolic processes (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: H3K27me3 is preferentially acquired on genes associated with transcriptional regulation, embryonic organ development, blastocyst formation, and metabolism.
source: GO term analysis revealed preferential acquisition of H3K27me3 on genes associated with transcriptional regulation, embryonic organ development, blastocyst formation, and metabolism (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Meiotic genes and those involved in immune responses are more likely targeted by H3K9me2.
source: On the other hand, meiotic genes and those involved in immune responses were more likely targeted by H3K9me2.
evidence: Based on GO term enrichment analysis comparing H3K9me2- and H3K27me3-marked genes.

claim: Different functional pathways are inactivated via establishment of distinct epigenetic states (H3K9me2 vs H3K27me3).
source: This analysis reveals that different functional pathways are inactivated via establishment of distinct epigenetic states.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 target different functional gene categories.

claim: There are little differences in the distribution of H3K9me2 between E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs.
source: Global and metagene analysis revealed little differences in the distribution of H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 between E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs (Figure 4A,D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A,D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Over 97% of genes marked by H3K9me2 show enrichment in both E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs.
source: Similarly, over 97% of genes marked by H3K9me2 showed enrichment in both cell types (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: H3K27me3 undergoes significant rearrangement in EpiSCs when compared with in vivo epiblast cells.
source: On the other hand, H3K27me3 underwent a significant rearrangement in EpiSCs when compared with in vivo epiblast cells, with genes regulating meiosis and bone development preferentially losing H3K27me3 at promoters (Figure 4E,F,H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F,H.

claim: Genes regulating meiosis and bone development preferentially lose H3K27me3 at promoters in EpiSCs.
source: On the other hand, H3K27me3 underwent a significant rearrangement in EpiSCs when compared with in vivo epiblast cells, with genes regulating meiosis and bone development preferentially losing H3K27me3 at promoters (Figure 4E,F,H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E,F,H.

claim: EpiSCs show a ~10% increase in global DNA methylation levels compared to E6.25 epiblast.
source: Indeed, our whole genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBSeq) of EpiSCs revealed a ~10% increase in global DNA methylation levels (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by WGBSeq data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Promoters that lost H3K27me3 acquired significantly more 5meC in EpiSCs.
source: More specifically, promoters that had lost H3K27me3 acquired significantly more 5meC in EpiSCs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: EpiSC derivation leads to an aberrant epigenetic state, especially at germline promoters.
source: This observation indicates that EpiSC derivation leads to an aberrant epigenetic state, especially at germline promoters.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that germline genes lose H3K27me3 and gain DNA methylation in EpiSCs.

claim: Stable silencing of germline genes might contribute to reduced competence of EpiSC for PGC fate.
source: Such stable silencing of these genes might contribute to a reduced competence of EpiSC for PGC fate.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation of aberrant epigenetic silencing of germline genes in EpiSCs.

claim: >97% of genes enriched with either H3K9me2 or H3K27me3 modifications do not exhibit differential expression in Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos.
source: We found that >97% of genes enriched with either H3K9me2 or H3K27me3 modifications do not exhibit differential expression in the Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ~63% of genes upregulated in Ezh2−/− show enrichment for H3K27me3.
source: Nevertheless, we found that ~63% of genes upregulated in Ezh2−/− and ~36% in Ehmt2−/− show enrichment for H3K27me3 and H3K9me2, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 1,2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 5—source data 1,2.

claim: ~36% of genes upregulated in Ehmt2−/− show enrichment for H3K9me2.
source: Nevertheless, we found that ~63% of genes upregulated in Ezh2−/− and ~36% in Ehmt2−/− show enrichment for H3K27me3 and H3K9me2, respectively (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5—source data 1,2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 5—source data 1,2.

claim: ~53% of genes upregulated in Ehmt2−/− are regulated by H3K9me2 deposition at the gene bodies.
source: In the case of Ehmt2−/−, a larger proportion (~53%) of genes seem to be regulated by H3K9me2 deposition at the gene bodies (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Direct G9a targets in the epiblast include Asz1, Casp14 and Cdkn1a.
source: Among direct G9a targets in the epiblast are Asz1, Casp14 and Cdkn1a, but not Otx2, or polycomb targets such as Hoxc10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Otx2 is not a direct G9a target in the epiblast.
source: Among direct G9a targets in the epiblast are Asz1, Casp14 and Cdkn1a, but not Otx2, or polycomb targets such as Hoxc10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Hoxc10 is not a direct G9a target in the epiblast.
source: Among direct G9a targets in the epiblast are Asz1, Casp14 and Cdkn1a, but not Otx2, or polycomb targets such as Hoxc10 (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There is rapid increase in H3K9me2 levels in primed cells at direct targets of G9a, including Asz1 promoter and Cdkn1a gene body.
source: The lcChIP-qPCR analysis showed rapid increase in H3K9me2 levels in primed cells at direct targets of G9a, including Asz1 promoter and Cdkn1a gene body (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: G9a represses regulators of germline and cell proliferation.
source: Thus, our genome-wide dataset together with the analysis of single loci reveal that G9a represses regulators of germline and cell proliferation, and a subset of them accumulate H3K9me2 mark shortly after implantation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of G9a leads to upregulation of germline and cell proliferation genes that show H3K9me2 enrichment.

claim: A subset of G9a-repressed genes accumulate H3K9me2 mark shortly after implantation.
source: Thus, our genome-wide dataset together with the analysis of single loci reveal that G9a represses regulators of germline and cell proliferation, and a subset of them accumulate H3K9me2 mark shortly after implantation.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data showing rapid increase in H3K9me2 levels during EpiLC induction.

claim: ~15% of repeats show significant H3K9me2 enrichment in E6.25 epiblast.
source: We found that ~15% (4.8 × 105/3.3 × 106) and ~18% (4.8 × 105/2.6 × 106) of repeats show significant H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 enrichment, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ~18% of repeats show significant H3K27me3 enrichment in E6.25 epiblast.
source: We found that ~15% (4.8 × 105/3.3 × 106) and ~18% (4.8 × 105/2.6 × 106) of repeats show significant H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 enrichment, respectively (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ~0.11% of all repeats are significantly upregulated in Ehmt2−/− epiblast.
source: On the other hand, only ~0.11% (3636/3.3 × 106) and ~0.06% (1646/2.6 × 106) of all repeats were significantly upregulated in Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− epiblast, respectively.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis of repeat elements.

claim: ~0.06% of all repeats are significantly upregulated in Ezh2−/− epiblast.
source: On the other hand, only ~0.11% (3636/3.3 × 106) and ~0.06% (1646/2.6 × 106) of all repeats were significantly upregulated in Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− epiblast, respectively.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis of repeat elements.

claim: 13/15 subfamilies repressed by G9a correspond to endogenous retroviral elements (ERV), especially ERV-L and ERV-LMaLR.
source: However, 13/15 subfamilies repressed by G9a are notable as they correspond to endogenous retroviral elements (ERV), especially ERV-L and ERV-LMaLR (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Single cell RT-qPCR from E6.25 Ehmt2−/− epiblast cells shows upregulation of MTD, MTEb and Lx8 but not IAP repeat elements.
source: Consistent with the RNA-seq analysis, single cell RT-qPCR from individual E6.25 Ehmt2+/+ or Ehmt2−/− epiblast cells showed upregulation of mouse transposon D (MTD), mouse transposable element b (MTEb ) and Lx8 but not of IAP repeat elements (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by single-cell RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Loss of G9a leads to significant depletion of H3K9me2 at MTEb and Lx8 loci, but not IAP.
source: Following TAM treatment, day 2 EpiLCs were used for lcChIP-qPCR, which showed significant depletion of H3K9me2 upon loss of G9a at MTEb and Lx8 loci, but not IAP (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: G9a deposits H3K9me2 at some repeat elements in postimplantation epiblast.
source: Thus, G9a deposits H3K9me2 at some repeat elements in postimplantation epiblast, where it is necessary to repress TEs that predominantly belong to the ERVs class.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of G9a leads to upregulation of specific repeat elements that show H3K9me2 enrichment.

claim: G9a is necessary to repress transposable elements that predominantly belong to the ERVs class.
source: Thus, G9a deposits H3K9me2 at some repeat elements in postimplantation epiblast, where it is necessary to repress TEs that predominantly belong to the ERVs class.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of G9a leads to upregulation of ERV elements.

claim: G9a has a potentially important role in maintaining genomic integrity.
source: This implies a potentially important role for G9a in maintaining genomic integrity.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation that G9a represses transposable elements.

claim: H3K9me2 modification accumulates rapidly in the postimplantation epiblast.
source: H3K9me2 modification, unlike H3K27me3, accumulates rapidly in the postimplantation epiblast (Figure 1B), preferentially in the intergenic regions where many cis regulatory elements reside (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me2 accumulates preferentially in the intergenic regions where many cis regulatory elements reside.
source: H3K9me2 modification, unlike H3K27me3, accumulates rapidly in the postimplantation epiblast (Figure 1B), preferentially in the intergenic regions where many cis regulatory elements reside (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Multiple putative enhancers show H3K9me2 enrichment in the epiblast.
source: Visual inspection of our lcChIP-seq analysis revealed that multiple putative enhancers show H3K9me2 enrichment in the epiblast, for example, in close proximity to Esrrb and Prdm1 (Figure 6A)
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-seq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is genome-wide accumulation of H3K9me2 in primed pluripotent cells.
source: Consistent with programming of epiblast in vivo by H3K9me2 modification (Figure 1B), we found genome-wide accumulation of H3K9me2 in primed pluripotent cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: There is increased enrichment of H3K9me2 at genes upon exit from naïve pluripotency.
source: Our analysis revealed increased enrichment of H3K9me2 at genes upon exit from naïve pluripotency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Significant H3K9me2 enrichment is observed at enhancers which show DNA hypermethylation and cluster separately from poised H3K27me3-enriched elements.
source: This effect extends to many enhancers but significant H3K9me2 enrichment is observed at elements, which show DNA hypermethylation and cluster separately from poised H3K27me3-enriched elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: H3K9me2 is not a distinct enhancer mark, but rather is associated with larger domains within which regulatory elements reside.
source: As with H3K27me3 modification, H3K9me2 is not a distinct enhancer mark, but rather is associated with larger domains within which regulatory elements reside (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ~12% of enhancers active in 2i/LIF ESCs gain H3K9me2 after 2 days of induction towards EpiLCs.
source: Interestingly, of all the enhancers that are active in 2i/LIF ESCs (p300, H3K4me1 and H3K27ac enrichment), ~12% (3884) gain H3K9me2 after 2 days of induction towards EpiLCs (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: ~3% of enhancers active in 2i/LIF ESCs become enriched for H3K27me3 after 2 days of induction towards EpiLCs.
source: Interestingly, of all the enhancers that are active in 2i/LIF ESCs (p300, H3K4me1 and H3K27ac enrichment), ~12% (3884) gain H3K9me2 after 2 days of induction towards EpiLCs (Figure 6B), while only 3% (1117) become enriched for H3K27me3.
evidence: Based on analysis of ChIP-seq data.

claim: Previously identified enhancer elements gain H3K9me2 in a G9a-dependent manner.
source: We confirmed that previously identified enhancer elements gain H3K9me2 in a G9a-dependent manner but active or H3K27me3 poised elements do not (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Active or H3K27me3 poised elements do not gain H3K9me2 in a G9a-dependent manner.
source: We confirmed that previously identified enhancer elements gain H3K9me2 in a G9a-dependent manner but active or H3K27me3 poised elements do not (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Acquisition of H3K9me2 occurs at distal regulatory elements.
source: Thus, acquisition of H3K9me2 occurs at distal regulatory elements, perhaps to direct or reinforce their inactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates at enhancer elements that become inactivated.

claim: H3K9me2-marked enhancers retain partial enrichment of active H3K27ac mark in EpiLCs, but exhibit near-complete H3K27ac loss in EpiSCs.
source: Notably, H3K9me2-marked enhancers retain partial enrichment of active H3K27ac mark in EpiLCs, but exhibit near-complete H3K27ac loss in EpiSCs (Figure 7A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: ~57% of H3K9me2-enriched enhancers in EpiLCs still retain significant H3K27ac.
source: Consistently, enhancer classification based on their epigenetic state has shown that ~57% (2212) of H3K9me2-enriched enhancers in EpiLCs still retain significant H3K27ac (Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: H3K9me2-enriched elements show dual H3K9me2 and H3K27ac enrichment.
source: To exclude possible effects of cell population heterogeneity, we performed sequential ChIP-qPCR, which showed dual H3K9me2 and H3K27ac enrichment (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by sequential ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Transient dual marking of enhancers by H3K9me2 and H3K27ac might indicate their continued responsiveness to signalling cues.
source: Such transient dual marking might indicate their continued responsiveness to signalling cues.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation of dual H3K9me2 and H3K27ac enrichment at enhancers.

claim: H3K9me2-enriched elements show no change in the active H3K27ac modification in EpiLCs lacking G9a.
source: In addition, H3K9me2-enriched elements showed no change in the active H3K27ac modification in EpiLCs lacking G9a (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by lcChIP-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The repressive H3K9me2 and activating H3K27ac modifications transiently co-occur at enhancers during epiblast priming.
source: Taken together, our findings show that the repressive H3K9me2 and activating H3K27ac modifications transiently co-occur at enhancers during epiblast priming.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2-marked enhancers retain H3K27ac in EpiLCs.

claim: Enhancers marked by H3K9me2 are in close proximity to repressed genes, both in the epiblast in vivo and EpiLCs in vitro.
source: We found that enhancers marked by H3K9me2 are in close proximity to repressed genes, both in the epiblast in vivo and EpiLCs in vitro (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Genes near H3K9me2-marked enhancers are enriched for regulators of apoptosis.
source: Consistent with the Ehmt2−/− embryonic phenotype affecting growth and development, these genes are enriched for the regulators of apoptosis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by GO term enrichment analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me2-marked enhancers show significant enrichment for regulators of early development (T and SOX2) and apoptosis (p53 and p63).
source: H3K9me2-marked enhancers showed significant enrichment for regulators of early development (T and SOX2) and apoptosis (p53 and p63) (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: H3K27me3 poised enhancers show enrichment for motifs of skeletal development regulators SOX9 and HOXD8.
source: In line with the PRC2 function, H3K27me3 poised enhancers showed enrichment for motifs of skeletal development regulators SOX9 and HOXD8 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: H3K27me3 and H3K9me2 accumulate at distinct enhancers that regulate early development.
source: Such non-overlapping motif signatures further validate that H3K27me3 and H3K9me2 accumulate at distinct enhancers that regulate early development.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2- and H3K27me3-marked enhancers show enrichment for different transcription factor motifs.

claim: H3K9me2-marked and H3K27me3-marked enhancers undergo robust transcriptional inactivation upon EpiLC induction.
source: We performed RT-qPCR for candidate robustly expressed eRNAs originating from regions enriched for H3K9me2 or H3K27me3. Upon EpiLC induction, such elements underwent robust transcriptional inactivation (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data for eRNAs shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Enhancers for genes linked with primed pluripotency show increased eRNA expression in EpiLCs.
source: This is not a global effect because enhancers for genes, such as Otx2 that are linked with primed pluripotency, show increased eRNA expression in EpiLCs (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data for eRNAs shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Upon blastocyst implantation, H3K9me2 domains extend to active enhancers targeted for initiation of silencing.
source: Thus, upon blastocyst implantation, H3K9me2 domains extend to active enhancers targeted for initiation of silencing, which accounts for the co-enrichment with H3K27ac.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates at enhancers that retain H3K27ac but show reduced eRNA expression.

claim: Loss of G9a leads to increased eRNA expression at 4 of 8 H3K9me2-marked enhancers in day 2 EpiLCs.
source: Following TAM treatment, day 2 EpiLCs showed increased eRNA expression at 4 of 8 previously identified H3K9me2-marked enhancers, confirming that, in principle, this histone modification promotes repression of enhancer activity (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells shown in Figure 8E.

claim: H3K9me2 promotes repression of enhancer activity.
source: Following TAM treatment, day 2 EpiLCs showed increased eRNA expression at 4 of 8 previously identified H3K9me2-marked enhancers, confirming that, in principle, this histone modification promotes repression of enhancer activity (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells showing increased eRNA expression upon loss of G9a, shown in Figure 8E.

claim: H3K27me3-enriched and active regulatory elements are unaffected by loss of G9a.
source: This was specific to H3K9me2, since the H3K27me3-enriched and active regulatory elements were unaffected (Figure 8E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from Ehmt2 knockout cells shown in Figure 8E.

claim: 4 of 7 eRNAs associated with H3K9me2 marked enhancers show significant increase in expression in Ehmt2−/− E6.25 epiblasts.
source: We were able to detect 7/8 eRNAs associated with H3K9me2 marked enhancers, and 4 of these showed significant increase in expression in Ehmt2−/− embryos (Figure 8F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from individual Ehmt2−/− epiblasts shown in Figure 8F.

claim: Control eRNAs do not show altered expression in Ehmt2−/− E6.25 epiblasts.
source: Of all four control eRNAs detected in vivo, none showed altered expression.
evidence: Based on RT-qPCR data from individual Ehmt2−/− epiblasts.

claim: G9a contributes to transcriptional and epigenetic repression of a subset of enhancers.
source: Taken together, these results reveal that G9a contributes to transcriptional and epigenetic repression of a subset of enhancers.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that loss of G9a leads to increased eRNA expression at H3K9me2-marked enhancers.

claim: Enhancers repressed by G9a are typically active in naïve pluripotent cells but become repressed during priming of the epiblast.
source: These elements are typically active in naïve pluripotent cells but become repressed during priming of the epiblast.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2-marked enhancers are active in 2i/LIF ESCs but show reduced eRNA expression in EpiLCs.

claim: Global H3K9me2 is established by a wave of G9a activity during early postimplantation development.
source: We present here evidence that global H3K9me2 is established by a wave of G9a activity during early postimplantation development and contributes to establishing a crucial chromatin signature at promoters and gene bodies.
evidence: Based on the observation of increased H3K9me2 and G9a levels in postimplantation epiblast.

claim: H3K9me2 contributes to establishing a crucial chromatin signature at promoters and gene bodies.
source: We present here evidence that global H3K9me2 is established by a wave of G9a activity during early postimplantation development and contributes to establishing a crucial chromatin signature at promoters and gene bodies.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates at promoters and gene bodies and is associated with gene repression.

claim: Once acquired, H3K9me2 represses a specific subset of genes, including key regulators of proliferation and germline development.
source: Once acquired, H3K9me2 represses a specific subset of genes, including key regulators of proliferation and germline development.
evidence: Based on the observation that loss of G9a leads to upregulation of proliferation and germline genes.

claim: The enrichment of H3K9me2 extends into domains that contain multiple enhancer elements, leading to their developmentally-linked inactivation.
source: The enrichment of H3K9me2 additionally extends into domains that contain multiple enhancer elements, leading to their developmentally-linked inactivation.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates at enhancers that become inactivated during development.

claim: G9a has an important role in setting the regulatory circuitry in the epiblast that enables the subsequent developmental programme to unfold.
source: This uncovers an important role for G9a in setting the regulatory circuitry in the epiblast that enables the subsequent developmental programme to unfold.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that G9a regulates genes and enhancers involved in key developmental processes.

claim: A wave of heterochromatization occurs during early postimplantation development that contributes to the establishment of a specific 'primed' epigenetic state in epiblast cells.
source: A wave of heterochromatization occurs during early postimplantation development that contributes to the establishment of a specific 'primed' epigenetic state in epiblast cells (Borgel et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Borgel et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2010).

claim: G9a and PRC2 have independent functions in epigenetic programming.
source: While both G9a and PRC2 are involved in this epigenetic programming process, we found limited overlap between H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 targets or, indeed, between genes that were upregulated in Ezh2−/−and Ehmt2−/− mutant embryos. This indicates that they likely have independent functions, as observed in sESC, which is unrelated to the previously reported G9a-dependent recruitment of PRC2 complex (Lienert et al., 2011; Mozzetta et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of limited overlap between H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 targets and upregulated genes in Ehmt2−/− and Ezh2−/− embryos, with citations to published work (Lienert et al., 2011; Mozzetta et al., 2013).

claim: Prior to gastrulation, H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 generate distinct repressive chromatin states, linked to DNA hyper- and hypomethylation, respectively.
source: Thus, prior to gastrulation, H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 generate distinct repressive chromatin states, linked to DNA hyper- and hypomethylation, respectively.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 are associated with high and low DNA methylation levels, respectively.

claim: H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 act as complementary systems to target specific regulatory pathways, ensuring that they become repressed during the exit from naïve pluripotency.
source: These modifications therefore act as complementary systems to target specific regulatory pathways, ensuring that they become repressed during the exit from naïve pluripotency.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 and H3K27me3 target different functional gene categories.

claim: Following PGC specification, there is germline-specific resetting of the epigenome, including the erasure of H3K9me2 and DNA methylation.
source: Following PGC specification, however, there is germline-specific resetting of the epigenome, including the erasure of H3K9me2 and DNA methylation (Hajkova et al., 2002; Seki et al., 2005; 2007), which allows for the expression of germline-specific genes that have been silenced by these epigenetic modifications.
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Hajkova et al., 2002; Seki et al., 2005; 2007).

claim: Erasure of H3K9me2 and DNA methylation in PGCs allows for the expression of germline-specific genes that have been silenced by these epigenetic modifications.
source: Following PGC specification, however, there is germline-specific resetting of the epigenome, including the erasure of H3K9me2 and DNA methylation (Hajkova et al., 2002; Seki et al., 2005; 2007), which allows for the expression of germline-specific genes that have been silenced by these epigenetic modifications.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2 and DNA methylation repress germline genes, and their erasure in PGCs would allow gene expression.

claim: E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs show highly similar distribution of H3K9me2.
source: We have characterised the epigenetic landscape of the in vivo primed pluripotent cells relative to its in vitro model represented by EpiSCs. It is noteworthy that the two cell types show highly similar distribution of H3K9me2
evidence: Based on comparison of ChIP-seq data from E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs.

claim: EpiSCs globally gain DNA methylation compared to E6.25 epiblast.
source: It is noteworthy that the two cell types show highly similar distribution of H3K9me2, but EpiSCs globally gain DNA methylation and lose H3K27me3 from germline-related genes, which might contribute to the reduced competence of EpiSCs towards PGCs.
evidence: Based on WGBSeq data comparing E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs.

claim: EpiSCs lose H3K27me3 from germline-related genes.
source: It is noteworthy that the two cell types show highly similar distribution of H3K9me2, but EpiSCs globally gain DNA methylation and lose H3K27me3 from germline-related genes, which might contribute to the reduced competence of EpiSCs towards PGCs.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data comparing E6.25 epiblast and EpiSCs.

claim: Loss of H3K27me3 and gain of DNA methylation at germline genes might contribute to the reduced competence of EpiSCs towards PGCs.
source: It is noteworthy that the two cell types show highly similar distribution of H3K9me2, but EpiSCs globally gain DNA methylation and lose H3K27me3 from germline-related genes, which might contribute to the reduced competence of EpiSCs towards PGCs.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation of aberrant epigenetic state at germline genes in EpiSCs.

claim: Stable promoter DNA methylation has been previously reported for two germline genes, Stella and Rex1.
source: Indeed, stable promoter DNA methylation has been previously reported for two germline genes, Stella and Rex1 (Bao et al., 2009; Hayashi and Surani, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Bao et al., 2009; Hayashi and Surani, 2009).

claim: In vitro derivation and self-renewal promotes aberrant accumulation of epigenetic modifications.
source: Thus we show that in vitro derivation and self-renewal promotes aberrant accumulation of epigenetic modifications, as is the case with sESC and hematopoietic stem cells (Ludwig et al., 2014; Weidner et al., 2013).
evidence: Inferred from the observation of aberrant epigenetic state in EpiSCs, with citations to published work (Ludwig et al., 2014; Weidner et al., 2013).

claim: Enhancer elements acquire H3K4me1 and H3K27ac coincident with their developmental activation.
source: It is established that enhancer elements acquire H3K4me1 and H3K27ac coincident with their developmental activation at this point, while others become poised and enriched for H3K27me3 (Buecker et al., 2014; Factor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Buecker et al., 2014; Factor et al., 2014).

claim: Some enhancers become poised and enriched for H3K27me3.
source: It is established that enhancer elements acquire H3K4me1 and H3K27ac coincident with their developmental activation at this point, while others become poised and enriched for H3K27me3 (Buecker et al., 2014; Factor et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Buecker et al., 2014; Factor et al., 2014).

claim: G9a is involved in the rapid switching of epigenetic states at regulatory elements by depositing H3K9me2.
source: We additionally reveal that G9a is involved in the rapid switching of epigenetic states at regulatory elements by depositing H3K9me2 (Figure 9).
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates rapidly at enhancers during EpiLC induction, supported by Figure 9.

claim: The accumulation of H3K9me2 at enhancers is mostly linked with transcriptional repression.
source: The accumulation of H3K9me2 at enhancers is mostly linked with transcriptional repression, although they transiently retain significant levels of H3K27ac.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2-marked enhancers show reduced eRNA expression despite retaining H3K27ac.

claim: Loss of an active epigenetic signature is often secondary to enhancer inactivation.
source: Thus, we show uncoupling of histone acetylation from the transcriptional state, which indicates that loss of an active epigenetic signature is often secondary to enhancer inactivation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that H3K9me2-marked enhancers show reduced eRNA expression while retaining H3K27ac.

claim: Contrasting epigenetic marks at enhancers might confer responsiveness and plasticity of cells to signalling cues.
source: Such contrasting epigenetic marks at enhancers might confer responsiveness and plasticity of cells to signalling cues.
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation of dual H3K9me2 and H3K27ac enrichment at enhancers.

claim: The dual marking of enhancers coincides with the rapidly unfolding developmental programme in postimplantation epiblast, resulting in potential for diverse cell fate decisions.
source: This coincides with the rapidly unfolding developmental programme in postimplantation epiblast, resulting in potential for diverse cell fate decisions.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that dual marking occurs during a critical developmental period.

claim: Loss of H3K9me2 at an oestrogen-induced enhancer in breast cancer cells promotes reactivation of the apoptosis regulator bcl2.
source: In line with this role, the loss of H3K9me2, as seen at an oestrogen-induced enhancer in breast cancer cells, promotes reactivation of the apoptosis regulator bcl2 (Perillo et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to published work (Perillo et al., 2008).

claim: The regulation of enhancer elements likely contributes to the phenotype of G9a null embryos.
source: The regulation of enhancer elements likely contributes to the phenotype of G9a null embryos, but is unrelated to increased expression of pluripotency genes, contrary to a previous suggestion (Yamamizu et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that G9a regulates enhancers and genes involved in development, with citation to a previous report (Yamamizu et al., 2012).

claim: Decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis in G9a null embryos is more likely due to de-repression of negative regulators of cell cycle, including Cdkn1a.
source: Decreased proliferation and increased apoptosis is more likely due to de-repression of negative regulators of cell cycle, including a potent cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor, Cdkn1a (also called p21).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Cdkn1a is upregulated in Ehmt2−/− embryos.

claim: G9a preferentially represses three clusters of X-linked genes: Rhox, Xlr and Mage-a.
source: Furthermore, G9a preferentially represses three clusters of X-linked genes: Rhox, Xlr and Mage-a.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data showing upregulation of these gene clusters in Ehmt2−/− embryos.

claim: Two of the X-linked gene clusters repressed by G9a are imprinted.
source: Two of these are imprinted, suggesting a role for H3K9me2 in this process, which merits further investigation (Maclean et al., 2011; Raefski and O'Neill, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published work (Maclean et al., 2011; Raefski and O'Neill, 2005).

claim: H3K9me2 may have a role in genomic imprinting.
source: Two of these are imprinted, suggesting a role for H3K9me2 in this process, which merits further investigation (Maclean et al., 2011; Raefski and O'Neill, 2005).
evidence: Speculative statement based on the observation that G9a represses imprinted gene clusters, with citations to published work (Maclean et al., 2011; Raefski and O'Neill, 2005).

claim: Pluripotency is a transient state during mammalian development that is established at the blastocyst stage.
source: Pluripotency is a transient state during mammalian development that is established at the blastocyst stage, and undergoes changes after implantation and development of the epiblast.
evidence: Based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Pluripotency undergoes changes after implantation and development of the epiblast.
source: Pluripotency is a transient state during mammalian development that is established at the blastocyst stage, and undergoes changes after implantation and development of the epiblast.
evidence: Based on established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: G9a-dependent programming entails spreading of H3K9me2 modification to enhancer elements where it regulates their activity.
source: Importantly, G9a-dependent programming entails spreading of H3K9me2 modification to enhancer elements where it regulates their activity; this contributes to rapid and dynamic changes at a critical period of epiblast development prior to gastrulation.
evidence: Based on the observation that H3K9me2 accumulates at enhancers and regulates their activity.

claim: G9a-dependent programming contributes to rapid and dynamic changes at a critical period of epiblast development prior to gastrulation.
source: Importantly, G9a-dependent programming entails spreading of H3K9me2 modification to enhancer elements where it regulates their activity; this contributes to rapid and dynamic changes at a critical period of epiblast development prior to gastrulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that G9a regulates enhancers and genes during epiblast development.
